name: Bonesmashing
lead: Bonesmashing (also bone smashing or face hammering) is a looksmaxxing practice in which people strike their own facial bones, typically with a hammer or similar object, in the belief that the resulting trauma will remodel the bone into a more defined, "chiselled" shape [1]. It belongs to the bonehacks category of looksmaxxing.

Wikipedia describes the practice as rarely carried out and as something of an inside joke, and notes that sources it cites classify it as misinformation [1]. It has nonetheless drawn attention from journalists and surgeons: letters in oral and maxillofacial surgery journals in 2024 described it as a dangerous trend spread on TikTok [2][3], and a 2026 cross-sectional study of social-media discourse recorded thousands of mentions of the term [4]. No clinical study has tested whether it changes facial structure.
infobox: Remodel facial bone (e.g. cheekbones, jaw, brow)
Surgeons warn of fracture and nerve injury [1][2]

paras: Practitioners strike areas such as the cheekbones, jaw or brow ridge with an object such as a hammer [1]. Looksmaxxing itself emerged in the 2010s on forums sometimes grouped as the PSL community, and Wikipedia does not identify where bonesmashing specifically began [1].

Proponents argue that bone responds to repeated micro-trauma by thickening or reshaping, and that visible changes in facial features follow. Threads on looksmaxxing forums include before-and-after posts credited to bonesmashing, while other members attribute the changes to puberty or editing [5][6].

No published study has measured bonesmashing outcomes in people. Surgeon commentary in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery expresses concern about the trend [2][3], and a 2026 study analysing posts on looksmaxxing and its soft and hard practices found that the term generated 2,518 mentions over twelve months with an estimated social-media reach of 32 million [4].

Facial surgeons cited in coverage summarised by Wikipedia warn of fractures, facial misalignment, neurovascular injury, deformity and changes to vision [1]. A nursing publication also published an article on the risks of the trend [7].
Wikipedia lists coverage by Vice, The Daily Dot, CBS Baltimore and The Guardian between 2023 and 2024; CBS Baltimore described it as a dangerous TikTok beauty trend that surgeons warn against [1].

timeline.event: Media outlets begin covering bonesmashing as a social-media trend [1].
Surgeon letters and a nursing article warn about the trend [2][3][7].
Cross-sectional analysis of looksmaxxing social-media discourse published [4].

lore.intro: On looksmaxxing forums, bonesmashing is debated as to whether it works at all, with some members posting claimed results and others attributing them to puberty, angles or editing [5][6].

claims.claim: Hitting facial bones makes them grow or reshape ("it works").
claims.believers: Some forum members post progress photos and say bonesmashing changed their cheek, brow or jaw appearance [6].
claims.experts: No published study has examined whether striking facial bone changes its shape; surgeons warn of fracture and nerve injury [1][2].

claims.claim: Visible changes are caused by bonesmashing rather than puberty or other factors.
claims.believers: Posters sharing results credit the practice for changes over months [5].
claims.experts: Other forum members respond that apparent changes are mostly puberty or image manipulation [5]; no controlled data exist.

card.summary: Hitting your own facial bones to reshape them; no study supports it and surgeons warn of fractures and nerve damage.
card.note: Surgeons warn of fracture, nerve and vision injury.

quick.overview:
Bonesmashing means striking facial bones, often with a hammer, in the hope of remodeling them into a sharper shape. It is a bonehacks practice in looksmaxxing, and Wikipedia says it is rarely actually done.

No clinical study has tested it. Surgeons have published letters warning about it as a social-media trend.
quick.mechanism: Believers say repeated impact stimulates bone to remodel. This mechanism has not been studied in the context of facial aesthetics.
quick.risks: Surgeons cite fractures, misalignment, neurovascular injury, deformity and vision changes as possible outcomes.
